title: Buying Your First Home in Québec

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Dreaming of buying your first home but feeling lost in the steps, costs and jargon? This guide is for you. It walks you through the entire journey, with the Québec-specific details that generic guides miss.

You will learn how much you really need (not just the down payment), how to finance your purchase, which steps to follow and in what order, and where the local pitfalls are — and how to avoid them.

After each chapter, a full-page lined 'My Notes' section lets you record your numbers and questions. That is how this guide becomes YOUR plan.

chapters.title: Are you ready to buy?
chapters.objective: Honestly assess your ability to buy before falling in love with a property.
chapters.html:
Honestly assess your ability to buy before falling in love with a property.

A solid purchase rests on three pillars: the down payment (the cash you put in), your borrowing capacity (how much a lender will approve based on income, debts and credit), and your ability to carry the ongoing costs of ownership without strain.

The true cost of owning

  • Municipal and school taxes (often several hundred dollars a month).
  • Home insurance.
  • Condo fees if applicable (operating fund + contingency fund).
  • Energy (Hydro-Québec, heating).
  • Maintenance reserve: budget roughly 1% of the property value per year.

Lenders review two ratios (GDS and TDS) and your credit score. Paying down credit-card debt before buying often boosts your borrowing capacity more than saving a bit more cash.

Le conseil d'Émilie

Never shop for a property before running your numbers. Starting with your budget is what makes the search enjoyable instead of stressful.

chapters.title: Funding your down payment
chapters.objective: Gather your down payment using every available tool.
chapters.html:
Gather your down payment using every available tool.

Minimum down payment depends on price (2026 edition, to confirm): 5% up to $500,000, 10% on the portion from $500,000 to $999,999, and 20% at $1,000,000 and up. Below 20%, mortgage-loan insurance (CMHC, Sagen, Canada Guaranty) applies and is added to your loan.

  • FHSA: contributions are tax-deductible AND withdrawals for a first home are tax-free (about $8,000/year, up to $40,000 lifetime, to confirm).
  • HBP (RRSP Home Buyers' Plan): withdraw up to $60,000 per person, tax-free upfront, repaid over 15 years (to confirm).
  • Family gift: accepted as down payment with a gift letter confirming it is not a loan.
  • FHSA and HBP can be combined for a first purchase.
Le conseil d'Émilie

Meet a mortgage broker BEFORE withdrawing anything. The order and timing of FHSA vs RRSP withdrawals has a real tax impact.

chapters.title: Mortgage pre-approval
chapters.objective: Get a confirmed amount and a rate hold before you shop.
chapters.html:
Get a confirmed amount and a rate hold before you shop.

Pre-qualification is a quick estimate with no verification. Pre-approval is different: the lender reviews your documents and confirms an amount plus a guaranteed rate for a period (often 90 to 120 days). That is what gives your offers weight.

Lenders qualify you at a rate higher than your actual rate (the stress test) to ensure you could absorb an increase, so your approved amount may be more conservative than expected — that is a protection. A mortgage broker shops several lenders for you, often at no cost.

Le conseil d'Émilie

With a pre-approval in hand, you stop dreaming and start choosing. In a fast market, it can be the difference between winning a home and watching it go.

chapters.title: Visiting, inspecting and making an offer
chapters.objective: See past the décor and make a solid, protected offer.
chapters.html:
See past the décor and make a solid, protected offer.

During visits, look at structure, not furniture: cracks, basement moisture, roof age, windows, electrical panel, water heater and furnace age. Ask whether renovations were done with permits.

Québec-specific checks

  • Clay soils (Montréal, Laval, North Shore): movement and cracks.
  • Pyrite, aging French drain, buried oil tank, vermiculite (possible asbestos).
  • Always make your offer conditional on a professional inspection.

A promise to purchase is binding once accepted. Protective conditions (inspection, financing, review of documents) are legitimate exit doors. Price your offer from a comparative market analysis, not emotion, and set a firm maximum in advance.

Le conseil d'Émilie

A winning offer is not always the highest: it is often the cleanest — reasonable conditions, dates that suit the seller, solid financing. It reassures the seller as much as the price.

chapters.title: Closing and the Welcome Tax
chapters.objective: Understand the final stretch and avoid cost surprises.
chapters.html:
Understand the final stretch and avoid cost surprises.

In Québec, the deed of sale is signed before a notary, who verifies title, prepares the deeds, handles funds and registers the sale. Budget closing costs: notary fees, inspection, adjustments, possibly an updated certificate of location, and home insurance active on possession day.

The Welcome Tax (transfer duties)

A municipal tax billed a few weeks or months after purchase, calculated in brackets on the greater of the price paid or the adjusted municipal assessment. Montréal adds higher brackets on expensive properties. Always get an estimate BEFORE buying and set the money aside.

Le conseil d'Émilie

Set the Welcome Tax money aside on closing day, in a separate account. It usually arrives right after you've spent on moving — planning for it avoids the one bad memory of an otherwise great purchase.

chapters.title: Plan d'action
chapters.html:
Vos prochains pas, concrètement.

Cette semaine

  1. Calculate my real budget and check my credit score.
  2. Gather my financial documents.

D'ici 30 jours

  1. Meet a mortgage broker and get a pre-approval.
  2. Optimize FHSA and HBP with an advisor.
  3. Define my criteria and two target areas.

Ensuite

  1. Book a free consultation with Émilie to launch the search with a clear plan.

chapters.title: Ressources & lexique
chapters.html:
• GDS / TDS: debt ratios used by lenders.
  • FHSA: first-home savings account, deductible contributions and tax-free withdrawal.
  • HBP: RRSP Home Buyers' Plan, up to $60,000/person, repaid over 15 years.
  • Welcome Tax: municipal transfer duties, billed after purchase.
  • Certificate of location: surveyor's document describing the property.
  • OACIQ: body regulating real estate brokerage and protecting the public in Québec.

options: B) A rate higher than your actual rate
